[[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[ja:菟道稚郎子]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Uji no Wakiiratsuko]][[sn:ji no Wakiiratsuko]][[Category:qq]] {{infobox royalty | Name = Ujinowakiiratsuko (菟道稚郎子) | Multilingual Names = | Family Name / Title = | Image = Ujinowakiiratsuko.jpg | Image Size = 170px | Image Description = Ujinowakiiratsuko (from {{ill|Zenkeng Kojitsu|ja|前賢故実}}) | Relationship = 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} | Title = | Full Name = | Rank = {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} | Honorific = | Mark = | Date of Birth = Unknown | Place of Birth = | Date of Death = {{ill|Jinshin Year|ja|壬申}} Year | Place of Death = {{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}} | Date of Burial = Jinshin Year? | Burial Place = Uji Tomb ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}) | Spouse1 = (Not recorded) | Children = (Not recorded) | Father = {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} | Mother = Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛) | Position = }} {{Coordinates List}} '''Ujinowakiiratsuko''' (うじのわきいらつこ/うぢのわきいらつこ, birth year unknown – {{ill|Yang Water Monkey|ja|壬申}}The Jinshin Year corresponds to 2 years after Emperor Ōjin’s 41st year (at his death), and the year before Emperor Nintoku’s first year (at his accession), according to the Nihon Shoki.) was an ancient Japanese royal figure recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki and Nihon Shoki|ja|記紀}} and other sources. He was the 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} (noted as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} in the Nihon Shoki) and the half-brother of the 16th-generation {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}. == Overview == Ujinowakiiratsuko is a figure deeply associated with the Uji region—as the name “Ujidō” indicates, reflecting an ancient representation of Uji in {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|山城国}}, namely Uji (present-day {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}). It is said that he established the Ujidō Palace ({{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}}) in Uji, and his tomb is likewise traditionally located in Uji. He is recorded in many historical texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. Among these, a celebrated story recounts that although he was beloved by his father, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, and appointed as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}}, he committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the great prince (【仁徳天皇】) as an act of virtue. However, this narrative appears only in the Nihon Shoki; the Kojiki simply notes his premature death. In the accounts of Ujinowakiiratsuko in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, many peculiarities have been observed. Moreover, the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains an expression “Emperor Uji” referring to him. These interpretations have given rise to various theories, including the “Emperor Accession Theory” and the “Assassination Theory by Emperor Nintoku.” == Nomenclature == The recorded names differ among the texts. In this article the name is uniformly rendered as “Ujinowakiiratsuko.” * '''Uchi Nowakikirōko''' – as in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji''' – as in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}Nihon Shoki, Emperor Ōjin Annals. * Uji Wakirōko – as in the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|風土記}} {{ill|Itsubun|ja|逸文}} * Uji Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} * Ujinowakiiratsuko – as in an itsubun of the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}}From the “Bohai Envoy” itsubun in the Nihon Shoki as recorded in the “Ruiju Kokushi” – [{{NDLDC|950692/663}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Kokushi Taikei Ruiju Kokushi’], 1913, page 663. * Uji Wakahiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Udo Wakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Udo Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} {{ill|Shoryōryō|ja|諸陵寮}}Engishiki, Shoryōryō Uji Tomb section – [{{NDLDC|1273499/90}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Engishiki Vol. 4’], page 90. Besides these, the expression “Emperor Uji” in the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} is also understood to refer to Ujinowakiiratsuko{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji (Kokushi)|1982}}. === On “Uji” === The element “Uji / Uji” (莵道/宇遅) in the name is connected to the place name “Uji” in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, referring to the city of {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}}. In ancient times, “Uji” was variously rendered as “Uji,” “Uchidō,” or “Udo,” but it is believed that the form “Uji” became fixed during the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}Inoue Mitsurō, “Uji” (from Nihon Kodai-shi Daijiten, Yamato Shobo, 2006).. In the Kojiki it is recorded that his mother, Miyanushiyakahaime (宮主矢河枝比売), lived in Kibata (present-day Kibata, {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}), suggesting a deep connection between Ujinowakiiratsuko and that locality. Even today, the place name “Uchidō” remains in Uji City, though it is read as “Todō.” Regarding the place name “Uji,” the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|山城国風土記}} explains that the palace established by Ujinowakiiratsuko is the origin of the name, and that prior to this the area was called “Kono-kuni” (許乃国)Fudoki of Yamashiro Province, Itsubun “Uji” (from ‘Shirin Saiyōshō’), edited by Takeda Yūkichi – [{{NDLDC|1173165/139}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 139.. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} (in the annals of Emperor Suinin, Emperor Chūai, and Empress Jingū) already records the “Uji River” (referring to the {{ill|Yodo River|ja|淀川}}, also known as Uji River), this explanation is considered erroneous{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}, and it is thought rather that the name was adopted in reference to Ujinowakiiratsuko’s own association{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}. In modern times, both the geographical notion of an “inner” area (uchi) – an area enclosed by mountains on the north, east, and south and bordered on the west by a vast pond ({{ill|Kyogai Pond|ja|巨椋池}}) – and the political meaning of “uchi” as a center of regional power centered on Uji have been advanced as the origins of the name'Uji City History Vol. 1' (Uji City Office, 1973), pp. 204–205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northern edge of the Yamato state, relatively free from external influence, and both the legends of Ujinowakiiratsuko and the term “Emperor Uji” suggest that a distinct political authority once existed in Uji. There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the term “Uchidō” derives literally from “a path formed by a herd of rabbits” ({{ill|Usagi|ja|ウサギ}})Minakata Kumagusu [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/527_28271.html “Folk Customs and Legends Concerning Rabbits”] (from ‘Jūnishi Kō’, Iwanami Bunko, 1994, as available on Aozora Bunko).. === On “Iratsuko” === “Iratsuko (郎子)” is an honorific appended to the name. Although the term “Rōjo (Iratsume/Iratsuhime)” appears frequently in the historical texts (43 instances in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}), the usage of “Iratsuko” for Ujinowakiiratsuko occurs for only four individuals in the Kojiki{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}The other three are: the grandson of Emperor Ōjin (Ōrōko, also known as the son of [【意富富杼王】]), the crown prince of Emperor Nintoku (Hatabino Ōrōko, also known as Ōhishimo or Ōsōkō), and the crown prince of Emperor Keitai (Ōrōko).. This distinctive usage—neither the common “Mikoto” nor “Ō (king)” used for imperial heirs—has drawn scholarly attention. Some argue that “Iratsuko” may have been used as a nickname, while others see it as a counterpart to “Rōjo”{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}However, at present institutions such as {{ill|Uji Shrine|ja|宇治神社}} sometimes combine “Iratsuko” with “Mikoto,” rendering the name as “Ujinowakiiratsuko Mikoto.”. It is also noted that the element “Waki” preceding “Iratsuko” is considered a corruption of “Waka” (若){{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. == Genealogy == === Kojiki and Nihon Shoki === (The naming follows the first appearance in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with other texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ujinowakiiratsuko was born a prince to Emperor Ōjin and the consort Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛, also known as Miyanushiyakahaime or 宮主矢河枝比売) of the {{ill|Waerushi|ja|和珥氏}} (Maruni) clan{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, Emperor Ōjin Annals; {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, 2nd year, March entry.. His maternal sisters include {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|八田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime-miko or Yata Wakirōjo, later Empress) and Metori no Hime-miko (女鳥王). Ōsazaki ({{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}), born of Emperor Ōjin and {{ill|Nakatsuhime no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (also known as Nakatsuhime or Nakachihime), was his half-brother. In addition, a related figure is the daughter of Miyanishitakuya-hime’s sister, Onabe-hime (小甂媛), who became known as Ujinowakiiratsuko Onna (菟道稚郎女皇女). There is no record in the historical texts regarding the wife or children of Ujinowakiiratsuko. {{Imperial Tomb Era}}
 
'''Simplified Genealogical Chart''' : The chart is arranged from left to right. Solid lines represent biological offspring, dotted lines represent marital relationships, and numbers indicate the order of imperial accession. The representation is based on the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. {{familytree/start|style=font-size:100%}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||||||||||||01| 01=[[磐之媛命|{{color|#FC4E6B|磐之媛命}}]]（前皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||01||||||||}|-|-| 01=[[仲姫命|{{color|#FC4E6B|仲姫命}}]]（皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||}|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|01| 01=[[仁徳天皇|大鷦鷯尊]]（{{supra|16}} 仁徳天皇）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|01||||||:||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|高城入姫命}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|}|-|-|-|01||:||:| 01=[[大山守皇子]]}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||-|-|01|||||||:||:| 01={{supra|15}} [[応神天皇]]}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|:|||,|01||:||:| 01='''菟道稚郎子皇子'''}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|}|-|-|+|-|-|-|01|:| 01=[[八田皇女|{{color|#FC4E6B|八田皇女}}]]（後皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|:|||`|01||||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|雌鳥皇女}}（隼別皇子妃）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||,|*|01||||||||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|宮主宅媛}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|01|(|}|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|02| 01=［[[和珥氏]]］日触使主|02={{color|#FC4E6B|菟道稚郎女皇女}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||`|01| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|小甂媛}}}} {{familytree/end}}
{{clear}} === Sendai Old Jikihonki === In the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}}, Ujinowakiiratsuko is described as the son of Nigihayahi ({{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|ニギハヤヒ}}, progenitor of the Mononobe clan) and the consort Yamanashi-hime of the Mononobe clan (物部多遅摩連)’s daughter, as recorded in “Tenson Honki”Sendai Old Jikihonki, “Tenson Honki”. – [{{NDLDC|991097/152}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Kokushi Taikei Vol.7’], page 152.. Also, similar to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Yamanashi-hime is identified as the mother of both {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|矢田皇女}} and Metori no Hime-miko. In connection with this account, as will be discussed in the section “Uji-bu” below, the Uji clan (or Uji-bu) bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name is considered part of the Mononobe clan. This has led some to suggest that the description in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which give his mother as belonging to the Waerushi, may be erroneousOta Akira, ‘Seishi Kakei Daijiten’ (Kadokawa Shoten, 1963), “Uji-bu”, entry 11.. == Records == === Nihon Shoki === [[File:Uji.jpg|thumb|280px|right|{{center|{{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}}}{{small|It is said that Ujinowakiiratsuko and {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}} contended on the Uji River.}}]] According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, it is stated that after being taught the classics by Adoroki ({{ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐}}) and Ōnin ({{ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁}}) sent from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} (i.e. “to present tributes”), he was favored by his father the emperor{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Emperor Ōjin, 15th year, August entry and 16th year, March entry.. In the 28th year of Emperor Ōjin’s reign, he denounced an impolite inscription from {{ill|Goguryeo|ja|高句麗}} stating “the King of Goguryeo teaches Japan” and tore it up{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Emperor Ōjin, September entry of the 28th year.. In the 40th year of Emperor Ōjin’s reign, he was designated as Crown Prince in January{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, January entry of the 40th year.. The following year, after the emperor passed away, Ujinowakiiratsuko did not ascend to the throne; instead, he and his half-brother exchanged claims to the throne. During this period, his half-brother {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}}—resentful that he had not been made Crown Prince—raised an army to kill him. Ōsazaki perceived this plot early and warned Ujinowakiiratsuko; in turn, {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}} fell victim to Ujinowakiiratsuko’s stratagem. It is said that a poem was composed in honor of Ōyamamori Ōji’s remainsFor interpretation of the reading and kana, see the annotated and translated edition of the Nihon Shoki (Ishikawa et al., Shōgakukan, 1996).. {{Cquote|Chihayabito: At the crossing of Ujidō, the catalpa bow is raised—though my heart intends to strike, though my heart intends to seize, in this direction I recall you, and at the far end I recall my sister; unyielding in resolve, I think thus—sorrowfully, I think here—and without striking, so I come, the catalpa bow is raised.
''Chihayahito, uji no watari ni, wataride ni tateru, azusa yumimayumi, ikiramu to kokoro wa mohedo, itoramu to kokoro wa mohedo, moto e wa kimi o omoide, suwe e wa imo o omoide, iranakeku soko ni omoi, kanashikeku koko ni omoi, ikirazu sokuru, azusa yumimayumi''}} After this, Ujinowakiiratsuko took up residence in Ujidō Palace, and for three years the two half-brothers exchanged claims to the throne. Troubled by the prolonged interregnum, which he believed led to national disorder, Ujinowakiiratsuko decided to put an end to the deadlock by taking his own life. Ōsazaki, shocked and saddened, journeyed from {{ill|Naniwa|ja|難波}} to Ujidō Palace and performed a soul-invoking rite on his remains; at that moment, Ujinowakiiratsuko was revived, ordered that his sister {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|八田皇女}} be admitted into the inner palace, and then passed away once more{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, pre-accession section of Emperor Nintoku.. === Kojiki === In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, the narrative begins with the account of Miyanushiyakahaime (宮主矢河枝比売), describing how Emperor Ōjin met a maiden residing in Kibata (present-day Kibata, {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}), and thereafter Ujinowakiiratsuko was born. Thereafter, the account largely follows that of the Nihon Shoki. The poem composed in honor of Ōyamamori Ōji’s remains is nearly identicalFor interpretation of the reading and kana, see Kurano Kenshi’s annotated Kojiki (Iwanami Bunko, 1963).. However, regarding the succession, the Kojiki simply notes that Uchi Nowakikirōko (Ujinowakiiratsuko) died young, leading to Ōsazaki (Emperor Nintoku)’s accession. === Fudoki === In the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|山城国風土記}}, the palace where Ujinowakiiratsuko resided is recorded as “Kirihara no Highetamiya” (桐原日桁宮). It is further stated that the place name “Uji” originated from this palace, and that before this the area was known as “Kono-kuni” (許乃国)Fudoki of Yamashiro Province, Itsubun “Uji” (from ‘Shirin Saiyōshō’), edited by Takeda Yūkichi – [{{NDLDC|1173165/139}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 139.. In the {{ill|Fudoki of Harima Province|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}}, there is mention of “the era of Emperor Uji”Fudoki of Harima Province, Ibo-gun Ōyashiro Jō – edited by Takeda Yūkichi [{{NDLDC|1173165/102}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 102.; although no detailed record of his deeds is provided, this “Emperor Uji” is taken to refer to Ujinowakiiratsuko{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji (Kokushi)|1982}}. === Manyōshū === The {{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}} includes the following elegiac poem{{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, Volume 9, Poem 1795 – [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=09/1795 09/1795] (Manyōshū Search System, {{ill|Yamaguchi University|ja|山口大学}}).. {{Cquote|Elegy from the Uji Wakirōko Palace
My sisters, now on the peak of this tree, flourish—the Tsuma Pine as if to be seen by the ancients.
''Imoragari, imakinomine ni shigeritatsu, tsumamatsu no ki wa, furuhitomikemu''|20px||{{ill|Kakimoto Asomi Hito Maro|ja|柿本朝臣人麻呂}}’s anthology, Manyōshū, Volume 9, Poem 1795}} In this poem, the term “ancients” (古人) is interpreted as “the late” (i.e. the departed), referring to UjinowakiiratsukoKojima Kenshi et al., annotated translation of the Manyōshū III (Shōgakukan, 1978), pp. 433–434.. === Others === Other historical texts that mention Ujinowakiiratsuko include: * The {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} entry for the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【815】), June 27. *: An account regarding a man named Kayō Yōnen, who was moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko and desired burial rites (see section “Tomb” below). * An itsubun in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} from the 3rd year of {{ill|Tenchō|ja|天長}} (【826】), March 1 (recorded in the “Bohai Envoy” itsubun from the Ruiju Kokushi). *: In the context of Emperor Sagaa’s abdication in favor of Emperor Junna, a reference is made comparing the exchange of the throne between Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko. * The {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} entry for the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【840】), May 6. *: In discussing the scattering of Emperor Junna’s ashes, the tradition of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s remains being scattered is mentioned (see section “Tomb” below). * The {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} in the “Tenson Honki” section. *: An account concerning his origins (as detailed above). * The {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} (Shoryōryō section) includes an entry on the Uji Tomb (the tomb of Ujinowakiiratsuko). == Palace == [[File:Ujigami-jinja, honden.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|Uji Kamigami Shrine|ja|宇治上神社}} ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}})}}{{small|Site associated with Ujidō Palace (Kirihara no Highetamiya tradition).}}]] It is said that Ujinowakiiratsuko resided either in '''Ujidō Palace''' (うじのみや, as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}) or in '''Kirihara no Highetamiya''' (きりはらのひげたのみや, as in the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|山城国風土記}}). This location is identified with either the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Shrine|ja|宇治上神社}} ({{Coord|34|53|31.44|N|135|48|41.18|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Kamigami Shrine (Ujidō Palace tradition)}}) or the {{ill|Uji Shrine|ja|宇治神社}} ({{Coord|34|53|27.77|N|135|48|38.52|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Shrine (Ujidō Palace tradition)}})According to shrine rankings, {{Harvnb|Uji Kamigami Shrine (Heibonsha)|1981}} designates it as Uji Kamigami Shrine, while {{Harvnb|Uji (Kokushi)|1982}} designates it as Uji Shrine.. Together, these shrines appear in the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Names List|ja|延喜式神名帳}} as “two shrines of Uji Shrine in Uji District, Yamashiro Province,” and until the Meiji period they were regarded as a single entity known as “Uji Rikyu Meishin”{{Sfn|Uji Shrine (Heibonsha)|1981}}. Also, according to the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|山城国風土記}}, the establishment of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s palace is given as the origin of the place name “Uji.” However, as noted in the section “On Uji,” this explanation has been questioned. In the {{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, an entry “Ujidono Miyako (Uji no Miyako)” appears{{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, Volume 1, Poem 7 – [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=01/0007 01/0007] (Manyōshū Search System, {{ill|Yamaguchi University|ja|山口大学}}).; however, this refers to a provisional palace where {{ill|Nukata no Ōkimi|ja|額田王}} stayed during his visit to {{ill|Ōmi Province|ja|近江国}}Kojima Kenshi et al., annotated translation of the Manyōshū I (Shōgakukan, 1978), p. 68.. == Tomb == [[File:Maruyama Kofun (Uji), haisho.jpg|thumb|220px|{{center|Ujinowakiiratsuko (deified) Uji Tomb
({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}})}}]] The tomb is officially designated by the Imperial Household Agency as the '''Uji Tomb''' (うじのはか, {{ill|Uji Tomb|ja|宇治墓}}; {{ウィキ座標|34|53|50.88|N|135|48|18.49|E|region:JP-26|位置|name=Uji Tomb (of Ujinowakiiratsuko)}}) located at Todomaru Yamayama in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}Compiled by the Imperial Household Agency, ‘Reiho Yōran’ – [{{NDLDC|1237123/10}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, 1934], page 10.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}'Ryōbo Chikeizu-shūsei Shukushōban' by the Tomb Division of the Imperial Household Agency, Gakuseisha, 2014, p. 403.. In the style prescribed by the Imperial Household Agency, it is a front-and-back circular tumulus (zenpō-kōen-fun). The site is known as the Maruyama Kofun. === Records === Regarding Ujinowakiiratsuko’s funeral, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} records that he was interred on “Mount Ujidō”{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. Also, the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} entry for the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【840】) mentions that, following his final instructions, his remains were scattered{{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, Shōwa 7, May 6 entry.. In the 5th year of the {{ill|Enchō|ja|延長}} era (【927】), the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} (Shoryōryō section) records the tomb under the name “Uji Tomb,” describing its location in Uji District, Yamashiro Province with an area of 12 chō by 12 chō and three attached mounds, classifying it as a remote tomb{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. This description—12 chō (approximately 1.3 km square)—greatly exceeds that of Emperor Nintoku’s tomb at Daisenryō Kofun (approximately 870 m square). During the Meiji period, in the 22nd year (【1889】), the tomb was officially designated as the Maruyama Kofun, and since then it has been managed by the Imperial Household Agency. The site lies on the eastern bank of the {{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}, and before the Meiji era it was known as “Ukifune no Mori” (Forest of Floating Boats). Although some argued that this differs from the “mountain” referenced in the Nihon Shoki tradition, its zenpō-kōen-fun form led to its identification as the “Uji Tomb”{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. At the time of this designation, a nearby small tumulus was identified as an ancillary mound for the burial of a man named Kayō Yōnen{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. Kayō Yōnen is mentioned in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【815】), where it is recorded that while residing in Uji he was moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko and desired to become a subordinate official; subsequently, by imperial decree, he was permitted interment in the “Ryo-shita” area{{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}}, Kōnin 6, June 27 entry.. The designation of this ancillary mound is attributed to aligning the term “ryō” with Ujinowakiiratsuko’s tomb{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}, though some interpret it as part of Emperor Nintoku’s tomb'Chū Zensengendaigo' (Kodansha Academic Library, 2006), p. 372. (typically, “ryō” refers to an imperial tomb, while “haka” denotes a royal tomb). Regarding the tradition of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s remains being scattered, aside from the aforementioned record in the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} (as recorded by middle counselor Fujiwara Yoshino), no other historical text mentions it; hence its veracity remains unclearKida Sadayoshi [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001344/card49806.html “Cremation and the Great Treasury – Customs of Cremation, Bone Washing, and Scattering”] (first published in “Minzoku to Rekishi, Vol. 3, Issue 7”, 1919, as available on Aozora Bunko).Nakayama Tarō [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001420/card50271.html “Honchō Hentaizōrei-shi”] (first published in “Hanzaikagaku Zōkan, Special Issue on Anomalous Customs”, July 1931, as available on Aozora Bunko).. In the record, Ujinowakiiratsuko is said to have ordered his remains to be scattered “in accordance with later generations,” which some interpret as “carried out as later commanded,” while others see it as establishing a precedent that popularized the custom'Continued Post-Nihon Shoki Upper, Modern Japanese Translation' (Kodansha Academic Library, 2010), p. 348.. Furthermore, in the 5th year of {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}} (【691】) an imperial edict provided for three guardian posts at the tombs of meritorious kings, suggesting that at that time—concurrent with the compilation of the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}—there were moves to designate tombs based on records such as the {{ill|Teiki|ja|帝紀}} and {{ill|Kyūji|ja|旧辞}}. It has also been proposed that the designation of tombs for {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊}} (Ise), {{ill|Hikogose no Mikoto|ja|彦五瀬命}} (Kii), and {{ill|Ijino Mikoto|ja|五十瓊敷入彦命}} (Izumi), along with Ujinowakiiratsuko’s tomb (Yamashiro), was intended to form the four extremities of YamatoNintō Atsushi, “Chronology and Issues of the Gigantic Zenpō-kōen-fun as Derived from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki”, in Ancient Imperial Tomb Studies, Yōsensha, 2016, pp. 13–16.. == Considerations ==
'''Genealogy of Emperors from the 10th to the 25th Generation''' {{familytree/start|style=font-size:100%}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(10) {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(11) {{ill|Emperor Suinin|ja|垂仁天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(12) {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02| 01=○|02=(13) {{ill|Emperor Ninken|ja|成務天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(14) {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(15) {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02| 01=(16) {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}|02='''Uji'''}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|v|-|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02|03| 01=(17) {{ill|Emperor Renzong|ja|履中天皇}}|02=(18) {{ill|Emperor Hantoku|ja|反正天皇}}|03=(19) {{ill|Emperor Inkyo|ja|允恭天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|||||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01||||02|03| 01=○|02=(20) {{ill|Emperor Ankō|ja|安康天皇}}|03=(21) {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.|||!}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02|03| 01=(24) {{ill|Emperor Ninken|ja|仁賢天皇}}|02=(23) {{ill|Emperor Kenzō|ja|顕宗天皇}}|03=(22) {{ill|Emperor Seinei|ja|清寧天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(25) {{ill|Emperor Buretsu|ja|武烈天皇}}}} {{familytree/end}}
In the historical records concerning Ujinowakiiratsuko, although scenes of his employing stratagem against Ōyamamori Ōji appear, the portrayal of his suicide as an act of virtue in the Nihon Shoki is noted for its particularly Confucian overtones'Uji City History Vol. 1' (Uji City Office, 1973), p. 210.. Moreover, given his mother’s origin from the Waerushi, the unique appellation “Iratsuko,” and various expressions hinting at imperial succession, his portrayal is considered notably peculiar{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. Regarding these aspects, the descriptions of his premature death (in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}) or suicide (in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}) are seen as embellishments; some long-advanced theories propose that he was in fact overthrown by Emperor Nintoku, with an underlying conflict between the Waerushi and {{ill|Katsuragi Clan|ja|葛城氏}}A theory by Kanda Hideo (as cited in {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. Many theories supporting the “Assassination Theory by Emperor Nintoku” have followed{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}See Miura Yūji, “Colloquial Translation of the Kojiki Complete Edition” (Bungeishunju, 2002), p. 248, note (40)., with some scholars regarding the narrative as one that both honors the tradition of the Waerushi and links it to the construction of the sacred imperial image of Emperor NintokuA theory proposed by {{ill|Yoshii Iwao|ja|吉井巌}} (as cited in {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. === Accession Theory === In contrast to the view that regards Ujinowakiiratsuko as a secondary figure to Emperor Nintoku, there is an alternative scholarly perspective. While the term “Iratsuko” in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} is used in a manner distinct from that reserved for an imperial heir (i.e. “Mikoto”), expressions implying that he actually ascended the throne are also foundExpressions referring to his status prior to birth, the notion of yielding the realm, and terms such as “hyakkan” and “collapse” have been noted ({{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. This has led some researchers to argue that he was a “possible emperor” existing parallel to the official genealogical record, and that the historical facts not recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} should be taken into account{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. A similar case is seen with the figure known as “Emperor Iitoyo” (alternatively, {{ill|Oshinumino Iratume|ja|忍海郎女}}), suggesting potential links in narrative style{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. Moreover, the article on Ujinowakiiratsuko has been argued to rationalize a shift in imperial succession from a father–son to a brother–brother lineKanazawa Kazumi, “Uji Nowakikiratsuko and the ‘Ancient’” (Doctoral Dissertation Abstract, Showa Women’s University, 2009).. Outside of the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the account in the {{ill|Fudoki of Harima Province|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} referring to “Emperor Uji” has been used to argue that he indeed reigned.{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko (Ancient Clan)|2010}}Ota Akira, “Seishi Kakei Daijiten” (Kadokawa Shoten, 1963), “Uji-bu”, entry 1, Yamashiro’s Uji-bu section.. == Uji-bu == The administrative unit bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name, that is, the imperial department ({{ill|bu|ja|部民制}}) known as '''Uji-bu''' (うじぶ, also rendered as Uji-bu), is identified{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. The associated companion clan, the Uji-bu clan (also rendered as Uji-bu-shi, with the surname {{ill|Kubane|ja|姓}} being {{ill|Ren|ja|連}}), is attested in the historical records{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. In the {{ill|Shinsen Shinjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}, they appear under the divine branch for both {{ill|Kawachi Province|ja|河内国}} and {{ill|Izumi Province|ja|和泉国}}, and are said to be descendants of Ikagiro (伊香我色乎命) of the 6th-generation descendant of {{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|饒速日命}}{{ill|Shinsen Shinjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}, Kawachi Province, Divine Branch Uji-bu Ren entry; Izumi Province, Divine Branch Uji-bu Ren entry.. In the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}}, it is stated that Tabenasukune (多弁宿禰命), a 7th-generation descendant of Nigihayahi, was the progenitor of the Uji-bu clan. Although the names of these two clans do not appear in other historical texts, direct (unqualified) or non-surnamed individuals are also attested in provinces such as {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国}}, {{ill|Hitachi Province|ja|常陸国}}{{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, Yōrō 7, February 13 entry and {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, the 1st year of {{ill|Tenaō|ja|天応}}, January 15 entry in Hitachi’s Naka County, under the names “Uji-bu Naoarasayama” and “Uji-bu Zensei.” Also, the {{ill|Ōi Shrine|ja|大井神社}} in {{ill|Mito City|ja|水戸市}}, {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|ja|茨城県}}, is traditionally associated with the Uji-bu clan of Naka County ([http://www.ibaraki-jinjacho.jp/ibaraki/kenou/jinja/01042.html Ōi Shrine] <Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Shrines>)., as well as in {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|ja|下野国}}, {{ill|Ōmi Province|ja|近江国}}, {{ill|Echizen Province|ja|越前国}}, {{ill|Bizen Province|ja|備前国}}, {{ill|Sanuki Province|ja|讃岐国}}, and {{ill|Chikugo Province|ja|筑前国}}, spanning the nation{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. It should be noted that definitive evidence establishing Uji-bu as the designated imperial department bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name is lacking; indeed, the {{ill|Kokushi Daijiten (Showa Period)|ja|国史大辞典 (昭和時代)}} does not list it among the confirmed names{{ill|Kokushi Daijiten (Showa Period)|ja|国史大辞典 (昭和時代)}}. Furthermore, another clan bearing “Uji” in its name, known as the Uji clan (with the surname later becoming {{ill|Sukuné|ja|宿禰}}), is also said to be of the Mononobe lineage and is sometimes proposed as the managing clan for Uji-bu{{Sfn|Uji (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. == Footnotes == === Notes === {{reflist|group="note"}} === Original Texts === {{reflist|group="original"}} === Sources === {{reflist|2}} [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[ja:菟道稚郎子]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Uji no Wakiiratsuko]][[sn:ji no Wakiiratsuko]][[Category:qq]] {{infobox royalty | Name = Ujinowakiiratsuko (菟道稚郎子) | Multilingual Names = | Family Name / Title = | Image = Ujinowakiiratsuko.jpg | Image Size = 170px | Image Description = Ujinowakiiratsuko (from {{ill|Zenkeng Kojitsu|ja|前賢故実}}) | Relationship = 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} | Title = | Full Name = | Rank = {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} | Honorific = | Mark = | Date of Birth = Unknown | Place of Birth = | Date of Death = {{ill|Jinshin Year|ja|壬申}} Year | Place of Death = {{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}} | Date of Burial = Jinshin Year? | Burial Place = Uji Tomb ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}) | Spouse1 = (Not recorded) | Children = (Not recorded) | Father = {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} | Mother = Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛) | Position = }} {{Coordinates List}} '''Ujinowakiiratsuko''' (うじのわきいらつこ/うぢのわきいらつこ, birth year unknown – {{ill|Yang Water Monkey|ja|壬申}}The Jinshin Year corresponds to 2 years after Emperor Ōjin’s 41st year (at his death), and the year before Emperor Nintoku’s first year (at his accession), according to the Nihon Shoki.) was an ancient Japanese royal figure recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki and Nihon Shoki|ja|記紀}} and other sources. He was the 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} (noted as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} in the Nihon Shoki) and the half-brother of the 16th-generation {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}. == Overview == Ujinowakiiratsuko is a figure deeply associated with the Uji region—as the name “Ujidō” indicates, reflecting an ancient representation of Uji in {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province }}, namely Uji (present-day {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}). It is said that he established the Ujidō Palace ({{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}}) in Uji, and his tomb is likewise traditionally located in Uji. He is recorded in many historical texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. Among these, a celebrated story recounts that although he was beloved by his father, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, and appointed as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}}, he committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the great prince (【仁徳天皇】) as an act of virtue. However, this narrative appears only in the Nihon Shoki; the Kojiki simply notes his premature death. In the accounts of Ujinowakiiratsuko in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, many peculiarities have been observed. Moreover, the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains an expression “Emperor Uji” referring to him. These interpretations have given rise to various theories, including the “Emperor Accession Theory” and the “Assassination Theory by Emperor Nintoku.” == Nomenclature == The recorded names differ among the texts. In this article the name is uniformly rendered as “Ujinowakiiratsuko.” * '''Uchi Nowakikirōko''' – as in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji''' – as in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}Nihon Shoki, Emperor Ōjin Annals. * Uji Wakirōko – as in the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|風土記}} {{ill|Itsubun|ja|逸文}} * Uji Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} * Ujinowakiiratsuko – as in an itsubun of the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}}From the “Bohai Envoy” itsubun in the Nihon Shoki as recorded in the “Ruiju Kokushi” – [{{NDLDC|950692/663}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Kokushi Taikei Ruiju Kokushi’], 1913, page 663. * Uji Wakahiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Udo Wakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Udo Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} {{ill|Shoryōryō|ja|諸陵寮}}Engishiki, Shoryōryō Uji Tomb section – [{{NDLDC|1273499/90}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Engishiki Vol. 4’], page 90. Besides these, the expression “Emperor Uji” in the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} is also understood to refer to Ujinowakiiratsuko{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji (Kokushi)|1982}}. === On “Uji” === The element “Uji / Uji” (莵道/宇遅) in the name is connected to the place name “Uji” in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, referring to the city of {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}}. In ancient times, “Uji” was variously rendered as “Uji,” “Uchidō,” or “Udo,” but it is believed that the form “Uji” became fixed during the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}Inoue Mitsurō, “Uji” (from Nihon Kodai-shi Daijiten, Yamato Shobo, 2006).. In the Kojiki it is recorded that his mother, Miyanushiyakahaime (宮主矢河枝比売), lived in Kibata (present-day Kibata, {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}), suggesting a deep connection between Ujinowakiiratsuko and that locality. Even today, the place name “Uchidō” remains in Uji City, though it is read as “Todō.” Regarding the place name “Uji,” the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} explains that the palace established by Ujinowakiiratsuko is the origin of the name, and that prior to this the area was called “Kono-kuni” (許乃国)Fudoki of Yamashiro Province, Itsubun “Uji” (from ‘Shirin Saiyōshō’), edited by Takeda Yūkichi – [{{NDLDC|1173165/139}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 139.. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} (in the annals of Emperor Suinin, Emperor Chūai, and Empress Jingū) already records the “Uji River” (referring to the {{ill|Yodo River|ja|淀川}}, also known as Uji River), this explanation is considered erroneous{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}, and it is thought rather that the name was adopted in reference to Ujinowakiiratsuko’s own association{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}. In modern times, both the geographical notion of an “inner” area (uchi) – an area enclosed by mountains on the north, east, and south and bordered on the west by a vast pond ({{ill|Kyogai Pond|ja|巨椋池}}) – and the political meaning of “uchi” as a center of regional power centered on Uji have been advanced as the origins of the name'Uji City History Vol. 1' (Uji City Office, 1973), pp. 204–205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northern edge of the Yamato state, relatively free from external influence, and both the legends of Ujinowakiiratsuko and the term “Emperor Uji” suggest that a distinct political authority once existed in Uji. There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the term “Uchidō” derives literally from “a path formed by a herd of rabbits” ({{ill|Usagi|ja|ウサギ}})Minakata Kumagusu [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/527_28271.html “Folk Customs and Legends Concerning Rabbits”] (from ‘Jūnishi Kō’, Iwanami Bunko, 1994, as available on Aozora Bunko).. === On “Iratsuko” === “Iratsuko (郎子)” is an honorific appended to the name. Although the term “Rōjo (Iratsume/Iratsuhime)” appears frequently in the historical texts (43 instances in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}), the usage of “Iratsuko” for Ujinowakiiratsuko occurs for only four individuals in the Kojiki{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}The other three are: the grandson of Emperor Ōjin (Ōrōko, also known as the son of [【意富富杼王】]), the crown prince of Emperor Nintoku (Hatabino Ōrōko, also known as Ōhishimo or Ōsōkō), and the crown prince of Emperor Keitai (Ōrōko).. This distinctive usage—neither the common “Mikoto” nor “Ō (king)” used for imperial heirs—has drawn scholarly attention. Some argue that “Iratsuko” may have been used as a nickname, while others see it as a counterpart to “Rōjo”{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}However, at present institutions such as {{ill|Uji Shrine|ja|宇治神社}} sometimes combine “Iratsuko” with “Mikoto,” rendering the name as “Ujinowakiiratsuko Mikoto.”. It is also noted that the element “Waki” preceding “Iratsuko” is considered a corruption of “Waka” (若){{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. == Genealogy == === Kojiki and Nihon Shoki === (The naming follows the first appearance in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with other texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ujinowakiiratsuko was born a prince to Emperor Ōjin and the consort Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛, also known as Miyanushiyakahaime or 宮主矢河枝比売) of the {{ill|Waerushi|ja|和珥氏}} (Maruni) clan{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, Emperor Ōjin Annals; {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, 2nd year, March entry.. His maternal sisters include {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|八田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime-miko or Yata Wakirōjo, later Empress) and Metori no Hime-miko (女鳥王). Ōsazaki ({{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}), born of Emperor Ōjin and {{ill|Nakatsuhime no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (also known as Nakatsuhime or Nakachihime), was his half-brother. In addition, a related figure is the daughter of Miyanishitakuya-hime’s sister, Onabe-hime (小甂媛), who became known as Ujinowakiiratsuko Onna (菟道稚郎女皇女). There is no record in the historical texts regarding the wife or children of Ujinowakiiratsuko. {{Imperial Tomb Era}}
 
'''Simplified Genealogical Chart''' : The chart is arranged from left to right. Solid lines represent biological offspring, dotted lines represent marital relationships, and numbers indicate the order of imperial accession. The representation is based on the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. {{familytree/start|style=font-size:100%}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||||||||||||01| 01=[[磐之媛命|{{color|#FC4E6B|磐之媛命}}]]（前皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||01||||||||}|-|-| 01=[[仲姫命|{{color|#FC4E6B|仲姫命}}]]（皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||}|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|01| 01=[[仁徳天皇|大鷦鷯尊]]（{{supra|16}} 仁徳天皇）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|01||||||:||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|高城入姫命}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|}|-|-|-|01||:||:| 01=[[大山守皇子]]}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||-|-|01|||||||:||:| 01={{supra|15}} [[応神天皇]]}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|:|||,|01||:||:| 01='''菟道稚郎子皇子'''}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|}|-|-|+|-|-|-|01|:| 01=[[八田皇女|{{color|#FC4E6B|八田皇女}}]]（後皇后）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|||||:|:|||`|01||||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|雌鳥皇女}}（隼別皇子妃）}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||,|*|01||||||||:| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|宮主宅媛}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left|01|(|}|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|02| 01=［[[和珥氏]]］日触使主|02={{color|#FC4E6B|菟道稚郎女皇女}}}} {{familytree|border=0|boxstyle=text-align:left||||`|01| 01={{color|#FC4E6B|小甂媛}}}} {{familytree/end}}
{{clear}} === Sendai Old Jikihonki === In the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}}, Ujinowakiiratsuko is described as the son of Nigihayahi ({{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|ニギハヤヒ}}, progenitor of the Mononobe clan) and the consort Yamanashi-hime of the Mononobe clan (物部多遅摩連)’s daughter, as recorded in “Tenson Honki”Sendai Old Jikihonki, “Tenson Honki”. – [{{NDLDC|991097/152}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Kokushi Taikei Vol.7’], page 152.. Also, similar to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Yamanashi-hime is identified as the mother of both {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|矢田皇女}} and Metori no Hime-miko. In connection with this account, as will be discussed in the section “Uji-bu” below, the Uji clan (or Uji-bu) bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name is considered part of the Mononobe clan. This has led some to suggest that the description in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, which give his mother as belonging to the Waerushi, may be erroneousOta Akira, ‘Seishi Kakei Daijiten’ (Kadokawa Shoten, 1963), “Uji-bu”, entry 11.. == Records == === Nihon Shoki === [[File:Uji.jpg|thumb|280px|right|{{center|{{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}}}{{small|It is said that Ujinowakiiratsuko and {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}} contended on the Uji River.}}]] According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, it is stated that after being taught the classics by Adoroki ({{ill|Adochigi|ja|阿直岐}}) and Ōnin ({{ill|Ōnin|ja|王仁}}) sent from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} (i.e. “to present tributes”), he was favored by his father the emperor{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Emperor Ōjin, 15th year, August entry and 16th year, March entry.. In the 28th year of Emperor Ōjin’s reign, he denounced an impolite inscription from {{ill|Goguryeo|ja|高句麗}} stating “the King of Goguryeo teaches Japan” and tore it up{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Emperor Ōjin, September entry of the 28th year.. In the 40th year of Emperor Ōjin’s reign, he was designated as Crown Prince in January{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, January entry of the 40th year.. The following year, after the emperor passed away, Ujinowakiiratsuko did not ascend to the throne; instead, he and his half-brother exchanged claims to the throne. During this period, his half-brother {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}}—resentful that he had not been made Crown Prince—raised an army to kill him. Ōsazaki perceived this plot early and warned Ujinowakiiratsuko; in turn, {{ill|Ōyamamori Ōji|ja|大山守皇子}} fell victim to Ujinowakiiratsuko’s stratagem. It is said that a poem was composed in honor of Ōyamamori Ōji’s remainsFor interpretation of the reading and kana, see the annotated and translated edition of the Nihon Shoki (Ishikawa et al., Shōgakukan, 1996).. {{Cquote|Chihayabito: At the crossing of Ujidō, the catalpa bow is raised—though my heart intends to strike, though my heart intends to seize, in this direction I recall you, and at the far end I recall my sister; unyielding in resolve, I think thus—sorrowfully, I think here—and without striking, so I come, the catalpa bow is raised.
''Chihayahito, uji no watari ni, wataride ni tateru, azusa yumimayumi, ikiramu to kokoro wa mohedo, itoramu to kokoro wa mohedo, moto e wa kimi o omoide, suwe e wa imo o omoide, iranakeku soko ni omoi, kanashikeku koko ni omoi, ikirazu sokuru, azusa yumimayumi''}} After this, Ujinowakiiratsuko took up residence in Ujidō Palace, and for three years the two half-brothers exchanged claims to the throne. Troubled by the prolonged interregnum, which he believed led to national disorder, Ujinowakiiratsuko decided to put an end to the deadlock by taking his own life. Ōsazaki, shocked and saddened, journeyed from {{ill|Naniwa|ja|難波}} to Ujidō Palace and performed a soul-invoking rite on his remains; at that moment, Ujinowakiiratsuko was revived, ordered that his sister {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|八田皇女}} be admitted into the inner palace, and then passed away once more{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, pre-accession section of Emperor Nintoku.. === Kojiki === In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, the narrative begins with the account of Miyanushiyakahaime (宮主矢河枝比売), describing how Emperor Ōjin met a maiden residing in Kibata (present-day Kibata, {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}), and thereafter Ujinowakiiratsuko was born. Thereafter, the account largely follows that of the Nihon Shoki. The poem composed in honor of Ōyamamori Ōji’s remains is nearly identicalFor interpretation of the reading and kana, see Kurano Kenshi’s annotated Kojiki (Iwanami Bunko, 1963).. However, regarding the succession, the Kojiki simply notes that Uchi Nowakikirōko (Ujinowakiiratsuko) died young, leading to Ōsazaki (Emperor Nintoku)’s accession. === Fudoki === In the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}, the palace where Ujinowakiiratsuko resided is recorded as “Kirihara no Highetamiya” (桐原日桁宮). It is further stated that the place name “Uji” originated from this palace, and that before this the area was known as “Kono-kuni” (許乃国)Fudoki of Yamashiro Province, Itsubun “Uji” (from ‘Shirin Saiyōshō’), edited by Takeda Yūkichi – [{{NDLDC|1173165/139}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 139.. In the {{ill|Fudoki of Harima Province|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}}, there is mention of “the era of Emperor Uji”Fudoki of Harima Province, Ibo-gun Ōyashiro Jō – edited by Takeda Yūkichi [{{NDLDC|1173165/102}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 102.; although no detailed record of his deeds is provided, this “Emperor Uji” is taken to refer to Ujinowakiiratsuko{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji (Kokushi)|1982}}. === Manyōshū === The {{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}} includes the following elegiac poem{{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, Volume 9, Poem 1795 – [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=09/1795 09/1795] (Manyōshū Search System, {{ill|Yamaguchi University|ja|山口大学}}).. {{Cquote|Elegy from the Uji Wakirōko Palace
My sisters, now on the peak of this tree, flourish—the Tsuma Pine as if to be seen by the ancients.
''Imoragari, imakinomine ni shigeritatsu, tsumamatsu no ki wa, furuhitomikemu''|20px||{{ill|Kakimoto Asomi Hito Maro|ja|柿本朝臣人麻呂}}’s anthology, Manyōshū, Volume 9, Poem 1795}} In this poem, the term “ancients” (古人) is interpreted as “the late” (i.e. the departed), referring to UjinowakiiratsukoKojima Kenshi et al., annotated translation of the Manyōshū III (Shōgakukan, 1978), pp. 433–434.. === Others === Other historical texts that mention Ujinowakiiratsuko include: * The {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} entry for the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【815】), June 27. *: An account regarding a man named Kayō Yōnen, who was moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko and desired burial rites (see section “Tomb” below). * An itsubun in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} from the 3rd year of {{ill|Tenchō|ja|天長}} (【826】), March 1 (recorded in the “Bohai Envoy” itsubun from the Ruiju Kokushi). *: In the context of Emperor Sagaa’s abdication in favor of Emperor Junna, a reference is made comparing the exchange of the throne between Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko. * The {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} entry for the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【840】), May 6. *: In discussing the scattering of Emperor Junna’s ashes, the tradition of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s remains being scattered is mentioned (see section “Tomb” below). * The {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} in the “Tenson Honki” section. *: An account concerning his origins (as detailed above). * The {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} (Shoryōryō section) includes an entry on the Uji Tomb (the tomb of Ujinowakiiratsuko). == Palace == [[File:Ujigami-jinja, honden.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|Uji Kamigami Shrine|ja|宇治上神社}} ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}})}}{{small|Site associated with Ujidō Palace (Kirihara no Highetamiya tradition).}}]] It is said that Ujinowakiiratsuko resided either in '''Ujidō Palace''' (うじのみや, as recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}) or in '''Kirihara no Highetamiya''' (きりはらのひげたのみや, as in the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}). This location is identified with either the {{ill|Uji Kamigami Shrine|ja|宇治上神社}} ({{Coord|34|53|31.44|N|135|48|41.18|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Kamigami Shrine (Ujidō Palace tradition)}}) or the {{ill|Uji Shrine|ja|宇治神社}} ({{Coord|34|53|27.77|N|135|48|38.52|E|region:JP-26|name=Uji Shrine (Ujidō Palace tradition)}})According to shrine rankings, {{Harvnb|Uji Kamigami Shrine (Heibonsha)|1981}} designates it as Uji Kamigami Shrine, while {{Harvnb|Uji (Kokushi)|1982}} designates it as Uji Shrine.. Together, these shrines appear in the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Names List|ja|延喜式神名帳}} as “two shrines of Uji Shrine in Uji District, Yamashiro Province,” and until the Meiji period they were regarded as a single entity known as “Uji Rikyu Meishin”{{Sfn|Uji Shrine (Heibonsha)|1981}}. Also, according to the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}}, the establishment of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s palace is given as the origin of the place name “Uji.” However, as noted in the section “On Uji,” this explanation has been questioned. In the {{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, an entry “Ujidono Miyako (Uji no Miyako)” appears{{ill|Manyōshū|ja|万葉集}}, Volume 1, Poem 7 – [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka2.php?kekka=01/0007 01/0007] (Manyōshū Search System, {{ill|Yamaguchi University|ja|山口大学}}).; however, this refers to a provisional palace where {{ill|Nukata no Ōkimi|ja|額田王}} stayed during his visit to {{ill|Ōmi Province|ja|近江国}}Kojima Kenshi et al., annotated translation of the Manyōshū I (Shōgakukan, 1978), p. 68.. == Tomb == [[File:Maruyama Kofun (Uji), haisho.jpg|thumb|220px|{{center|Ujinowakiiratsuko (deified) Uji Tomb
({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}})}}]] The tomb is officially designated by the Imperial Household Agency as the '''Uji Tomb''' (うじのはか, {{ill|Uji Tomb|ja|宇治墓}}; {{ウィキ座標|34|53|50.88|N|135|48|18.49|E|region:JP-26|位置|name=Uji Tomb (of Ujinowakiiratsuko)}}) located at Todomaru Yamayama in {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}Compiled by the Imperial Household Agency, ‘Reiho Yōran’ – [{{NDLDC|1237123/10}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, 1934], page 10.{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}'Ryōbo Chikeizu-shūsei Shukushōban' by the Tomb Division of the Imperial Household Agency, Gakuseisha, 2014, p. 403.. In the style prescribed by the Imperial Household Agency, it is a front-and-back circular tumulus (zenpō-kōen-fun). The site is known as the Maruyama Kofun. === Records === Regarding Ujinowakiiratsuko’s funeral, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} records that he was interred on “Mount Ujidō”{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. Also, the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} entry for the 7th year of {{ill|Shōwa|ja|承和}} (【840】) mentions that, following his final instructions, his remains were scattered{{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, Shōwa 7, May 6 entry.. In the 5th year of the {{ill|Enchō|ja|延長}} era (【927】), the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} (Shoryōryō section) records the tomb under the name “Uji Tomb,” describing its location in Uji District, Yamashiro Province with an area of 12 chō by 12 chō and three attached mounds, classifying it as a remote tomb{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. This description—12 chō (approximately 1.3 km square)—greatly exceeds that of Emperor Nintoku’s tomb at Daisenryō Kofun (approximately 870 m square). During the Meiji period, in the 22nd year (【1889】), the tomb was officially designated as the Maruyama Kofun, and since then it has been managed by the Imperial Household Agency. The site lies on the eastern bank of the {{ill|Uji River|ja|宇治川}}, and before the Meiji era it was known as “Ukifune no Mori” (Forest of Floating Boats). Although some argued that this differs from the “mountain” referenced in the Nihon Shoki tradition, its zenpō-kōen-fun form led to its identification as the “Uji Tomb”{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. At the time of this designation, a nearby small tumulus was identified as an ancillary mound for the burial of a man named Kayō Yōnen{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}. Kayō Yōnen is mentioned in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} in the 6th year of {{ill|Kōnin|ja|弘仁}} (【815】), where it is recorded that while residing in Uji he was moved by the story of Emperor Nintoku and Ujinowakiiratsuko and desired to become a subordinate official; subsequently, by imperial decree, he was permitted interment in the “Ryo-shita” area{{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}}, Kōnin 6, June 27 entry.. The designation of this ancillary mound is attributed to aligning the term “ryō” with Ujinowakiiratsuko’s tomb{{Sfn|Uji Tomb (Kokushi)|1982}}, though some interpret it as part of Emperor Nintoku’s tomb'Chū Zensengendaigo' (Kodansha Academic Library, 2006), p. 372. (typically, “ryō” refers to an imperial tomb, while “haka” denotes a royal tomb). Regarding the tradition of Ujinowakiiratsuko’s remains being scattered, aside from the aforementioned record in the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} (as recorded by middle counselor Fujiwara Yoshino), no other historical text mentions it; hence its veracity remains unclearKida Sadayoshi [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001344/card49806.html “Cremation and the Great Treasury – Customs of Cremation, Bone Washing, and Scattering”] (first published in “Minzoku to Rekishi, Vol. 3, Issue 7”, 1919, as available on Aozora Bunko).Nakayama Tarō [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/001420/card50271.html “Honchō Hentaizōrei-shi”] (first published in “Hanzaikagaku Zōkan, Special Issue on Anomalous Customs”, July 1931, as available on Aozora Bunko).. In the record, Ujinowakiiratsuko is said to have ordered his remains to be scattered “in accordance with later generations,” which some interpret as “carried out as later commanded,” while others see it as establishing a precedent that popularized the custom'Continued Post-Nihon Shoki Upper, Modern Japanese Translation' (Kodansha Academic Library, 2010), p. 348.. Furthermore, in the 5th year of {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}} (【691】) an imperial edict provided for three guardian posts at the tombs of meritorious kings, suggesting that at that time—concurrent with the compilation of the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}—there were moves to designate tombs based on records such as the {{ill|Teiki|ja|帝紀}} and {{ill|Kyūji|ja|旧辞}}. It has also been proposed that the designation of tombs for {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊}} (Ise), {{ill|Hikogose no Mikoto|ja|彦五瀬命}} (Kii), and {{ill|Ijino Mikoto|ja|五十瓊敷入彦命}} (Izumi), along with Ujinowakiiratsuko’s tomb (Yamashiro), was intended to form the four extremities of YamatoNintō Atsushi, “Chronology and Issues of the Gigantic Zenpō-kōen-fun as Derived from the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki”, in Ancient Imperial Tomb Studies, Yōsensha, 2016, pp. 13–16.. == Considerations ==
'''Genealogy of Emperors from the 10th to the 25th Generation''' {{familytree/start|style=font-size:100%}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(10) {{ill|Emperor Sujin|ja|崇神天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(11) {{ill|Emperor Suinin|ja|垂仁天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(12) {{ill|Emperor Keikō|ja|景行天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02| 01=○|02=(13) {{ill|Emperor Ninken|ja|成務天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(14) {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(15) {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02| 01=(16) {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}|02='''Uji'''}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|v|-|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02|03| 01=(17) {{ill|Emperor Renzong|ja|履中天皇}}|02=(18) {{ill|Emperor Hantoku|ja|反正天皇}}|03=(19) {{ill|Emperor Inkyo|ja|允恭天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!|||||)|-|.}} {{familytree|border=0|01||||02|03| 01=○|02=(20) {{ill|Emperor Ankō|ja|安康天皇}}|03=(21) {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||)|-|.|||!}} {{familytree|border=0|01|02|03| 01=(24) {{ill|Emperor Ninken|ja|仁賢天皇}}|02=(23) {{ill|Emperor Kenzō|ja|顕宗天皇}}|03=(22) {{ill|Emperor Seinei|ja|清寧天皇}}}} {{familytree|border=0|||!}} {{familytree|border=0|01| 01=(25) {{ill|Emperor Buretsu|ja|武烈天皇}}}} {{familytree/end}}
In the historical records concerning Ujinowakiiratsuko, although scenes of his employing stratagem against Ōyamamori Ōji appear, the portrayal of his suicide as an act of virtue in the Nihon Shoki is noted for its particularly Confucian overtones'Uji City History Vol. 1' (Uji City Office, 1973), p. 210.. Moreover, given his mother’s origin from the Waerushi, the unique appellation “Iratsuko,” and various expressions hinting at imperial succession, his portrayal is considered notably peculiar{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. Regarding these aspects, the descriptions of his premature death (in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}) or suicide (in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}) are seen as embellishments; some long-advanced theories propose that he was in fact overthrown by Emperor Nintoku, with an underlying conflict between the Waerushi and {{ill|Katsuragi Clan|ja|葛城氏}}A theory by Kanda Hideo (as cited in {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. Many theories supporting the “Assassination Theory by Emperor Nintoku” have followed{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}See Miura Yūji, “Colloquial Translation of the Kojiki Complete Edition” (Bungeishunju, 2002), p. 248, note (40)., with some scholars regarding the narrative as one that both honors the tradition of the Waerushi and links it to the construction of the sacred imperial image of Emperor NintokuA theory proposed by {{ill|Yoshii Iwao|ja|吉井巌}} (as cited in {{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. === Accession Theory === In contrast to the view that regards Ujinowakiiratsuko as a secondary figure to Emperor Nintoku, there is an alternative scholarly perspective. While the term “Iratsuko” in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} is used in a manner distinct from that reserved for an imperial heir (i.e. “Mikoto”), expressions implying that he actually ascended the throne are also foundExpressions referring to his status prior to birth, the notion of yielding the realm, and terms such as “hyakkan” and “collapse” have been noted ({{Harv|Kanazawa|2007}}).. This has led some researchers to argue that he was a “possible emperor” existing parallel to the official genealogical record, and that the historical facts not recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} should be taken into account{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. A similar case is seen with the figure known as “Emperor Iitoyo” (alternatively, {{ill|Oshinumino Iratume|ja|忍海郎女}}), suggesting potential links in narrative style{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. Moreover, the article on Ujinowakiiratsuko has been argued to rationalize a shift in imperial succession from a father–son to a brother–brother lineKanazawa Kazumi, “Uji Nowakikiratsuko and the ‘Ancient’” (Doctoral Dissertation Abstract, Showa Women’s University, 2009).. Outside of the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, the account in the {{ill|Fudoki of Harima Province|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} referring to “Emperor Uji” has been used to argue that he indeed reigned.{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko (Ancient Clan)|2010}}Ota Akira, “Seishi Kakei Daijiten” (Kadokawa Shoten, 1963), “Uji-bu”, entry 1, Yamashiro’s Uji-bu section.. == Uji-bu == The administrative unit bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name, that is, the imperial department ({{ill|bu|ja|部民制}}) known as '''Uji-bu''' (うじぶ, also rendered as Uji-bu), is identified{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. The associated companion clan, the Uji-bu clan (also rendered as Uji-bu-shi, with the surname {{ill|Kubane|ja|姓}} being {{ill|Ren|ja|連}}), is attested in the historical records{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. In the {{ill|Shinsen Shinjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}, they appear under the divine branch for both {{ill|Kawachi Province|ja|河内国}} and {{ill|Izumi Province|ja|和泉国}}, and are said to be descendants of Ikagiro (伊香我色乎命) of the 6th-generation descendant of {{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|饒速日命}}{{ill|Shinsen Shinjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}, Kawachi Province, Divine Branch Uji-bu Ren entry; Izumi Province, Divine Branch Uji-bu Ren entry.. In the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}}, it is stated that Tabenasukune (多弁宿禰命), a 7th-generation descendant of Nigihayahi, was the progenitor of the Uji-bu clan. Although the names of these two clans do not appear in other historical texts, direct (unqualified) or non-surnamed individuals are also attested in provinces such as {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国}}, {{ill|Hitachi Province|ja|常陸国}}{{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, Yōrō 7, February 13 entry and {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}}, the 1st year of {{ill|Tenaō|ja|天応}}, January 15 entry in Hitachi’s Naka County, under the names “Uji-bu Naoarasayama” and “Uji-bu Zensei.” Also, the {{ill|Ōi Shrine|ja|大井神社}} in {{ill|Mito City|ja|水戸市}}, {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|ja|茨城県}}, is traditionally associated with the Uji-bu clan of Naka County ([http://www.ibaraki-jinjacho.jp/ibaraki/kenou/jinja/01042.html Ōi Shrine] <Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Shrines>)., as well as in {{ill|Shimotsuke Province|ja|下野国}}, {{ill|Ōmi Province|ja|近江国}}, {{ill|Echizen Province|ja|越前国}}, {{ill|Bizen Province|ja|備前国}}, {{ill|Sanuki Province|ja|讃岐国}}, and {{ill|Chikugo Province|ja|筑前国}}, spanning the nation{{Sfn|Uji-bu (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. It should be noted that definitive evidence establishing Uji-bu as the designated imperial department bearing Ujinowakiiratsuko’s name is lacking; indeed, the {{ill|Kokushi Daijiten (Showa Period)|ja|国史大辞典 (昭和時代)}} does not list it among the confirmed names{{ill|Kokushi Daijiten (Showa Period)|ja|国史大辞典 (昭和時代)}}. Furthermore, another clan bearing “Uji” in its name, known as the Uji clan (with the surname later becoming {{ill|Sukuné|ja|宿禰}}), is also said to be of the Mononobe lineage and is sometimes proposed as the managing clan for Uji-bu{{Sfn|Uji (Ancient Clan)|2010}}. == Footnotes == === Notes === {{reflist|group="note"}} === Original Texts === {{reflist|group="original"}} === Sources === {{reflist|2}} [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[ja:菟道稚郎子]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Uji no Wakiiratsuko]][[sn:ji no Wakiiratsuko]][[Category:11]] {{infobox royalty | Name = Ujinowakiiratsuko (菟道稚郎子) | Multilingual Names = | Family Name / Title = | Image = Ujinowakiiratsuko.jpg | Image Size = 170px | Image Description = Ujinowakiiratsuko (from {{ill|Zenkeng Kojitsu|ja|前賢故実}}) | Relationship = 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} | Title = | Full Name = | Rank = {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} | Honorific = | Mark = | Date of Birth = Unknown | Place of Birth = | Date of Death = {{ill|Jinshin Year|ja|壬申}} Year | Place of Death = {{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}} | Date of Burial = Jinshin Year? | Burial Place = Uji Tomb ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}) | Spouse1 = (Not recorded) | Children = (Not recorded) | Father = {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} | Mother = Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛) | Position = }} {{Coordinates List}} '''Ujinowakiiratsuko''' (うじのわきいらつこ/うぢのわきいらつこ, birth year unknown – {{ill|Yang Water Monkey|ja|壬申}}The Jinshin Year corresponds to 2 years after Emperor Ōjin’s 41st year (at his death), and the year before Emperor Nintoku’s first year (at his accession), according to the Nihon Shoki.) was an ancient Japanese royal figure recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki and Nihon Shoki|ja|記紀}} and other sources. He was the 15th-generation {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} {{ill|Imperial Prince|ja|皇子}} (noted as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}} in the Nihon Shoki) and the half-brother of the 16th-generation {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}. == Overview == Ujinowakiiratsuko is a figure deeply associated with the Uji region—as the name “Ujidō” indicates, reflecting an ancient representation of Uji in {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province }}, namely Uji (present-day {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}} {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}). It is said that he established the Ujidō Palace ({{ill|Ujidō Palace|ja|菟道宮}}) in Uji, and his tomb is likewise traditionally located in Uji. He is recorded in many historical texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}. Among these, a celebrated story recounts that although he was beloved by his father, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, and appointed as {{ill|Crown Prince|ja|皇太子}}, he committed suicide in order to cede the throne to his half-brother, the great prince (【仁徳天皇】) as an act of virtue. However, this narrative appears only in the Nihon Shoki; the Kojiki simply notes his premature death. In the accounts of Ujinowakiiratsuko in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, many peculiarities have been observed. Moreover, the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} contains an expression “Emperor Uji” referring to him. These interpretations have given rise to various theories, including the “Emperor Accession Theory” and the “Assassination Theory by Emperor Nintoku.” == Nomenclature == The recorded names differ among the texts. In this article the name is uniformly rendered as “Ujinowakiiratsuko.” * '''Uchi Nowakikirōko''' – as in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} * '''Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji''' – as in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}Nihon Shoki, Emperor Ōjin Annals. * Uji Wakirōko – as in the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|風土記}} {{ill|Itsubun|ja|逸文}} * Uji Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}} * Ujinowakiiratsuko – as in an itsubun of the {{ill|Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|日本後紀}}From the “Bohai Envoy” itsubun in the Nihon Shoki as recorded in the “Ruiju Kokushi” – [{{NDLDC|950692/663}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Kokushi Taikei Ruiju Kokushi’], 1913, page 663. * Uji Wakahiko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Continued Post-Nihon Shoki|ja|続日本後紀}} * Udo Wakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Udo Iratsuko – as in the {{ill|Sendai Old Jikihonki|ja|先代旧事本紀}} “Tenson Honki” * Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji – as in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} {{ill|Shoryōryō|ja|諸陵寮}}Engishiki, Shoryōryō Uji Tomb section – [{{NDLDC|1273499/90}} National Diet Library Digital Collection, ‘Engishiki Vol. 4’], page 90. Besides these, the expression “Emperor Uji” in the {{ill|Harima Province Fudoki|ja|播磨国風土記|1=Harima no Kuni Fudoki}} is also understood to refer to Ujinowakiiratsuko{{Sfn|Ujinowakiiratsuko Ōji (Kokushi)|1982}}. === On “Uji” === The element “Uji / Uji” (莵道/宇遅) in the name is connected to the place name “Uji” in southern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, referring to the city of {{ill|Uji|ja|宇治}}. In ancient times, “Uji” was variously rendered as “Uji,” “Uchidō,” or “Udo,” but it is believed that the form “Uji” became fixed during the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}Inoue Mitsurō, “Uji” (from Nihon Kodai-shi Daijiten, Yamato Shobo, 2006).. In the Kojiki it is recorded that his mother, Miyanushiyakahaime (宮主矢河枝比売), lived in Kibata (present-day Kibata, {{ill|Uji City|ja|宇治市}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}), suggesting a deep connection between Ujinowakiiratsuko and that locality. Even today, the place name “Uchidō” remains in Uji City, though it is read as “Todō.” Regarding the place name “Uji,” the itsubun of the {{ill|Fudoki of Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province 風土記}} explains that the palace established by Ujinowakiiratsuko is the origin of the name, and that prior to this the area was called “Kono-kuni” (許乃国)Fudoki of Yamashiro Province, Itsubun “Uji” (from ‘Shirin Saiyōshō’), edited by Takeda Yūkichi – [{{NDLDC|1173165/139}} Iwanami Shoten, 1937, National Diet Library Digital Collection], page 139.. However, since the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} (in the annals of Emperor Suinin, Emperor Chūai, and Empress Jingū) already records the “Uji River” (referring to the {{ill|Yodo River|ja|淀川}}, also known as Uji River), this explanation is considered erroneous{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}, and it is thought rather that the name was adopted in reference to Ujinowakiiratsuko’s own association{{Sfn|Uji (Kadokawa)|1982}}. In modern times, both the geographical notion of an “inner” area (uchi) – an area enclosed by mountains on the north, east, and south and bordered on the west by a vast pond ({{ill|Kyogai Pond|ja|巨椋池}}) – and the political meaning of “uchi” as a center of regional power centered on Uji have been advanced as the origins of the name'Uji City History Vol. 1' (Uji City Office, 1973), pp. 204–205.{{Sfn|Uji City (Heibonsha)|1981}}. In fact, Uji is located at the northern edge of the Yamato state, relatively free from external influence, and both the legends of Ujinowakiiratsuko and the term “Emperor Uji” suggest that a distinct political authority once existed in Uji. There is also a theory by {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}} that the term “Uchidō” derives literally from “a path formed by a herd of rabbits” ({{ill|Usagi|ja|ウサギ}})Minakata Kumagusu [https://www.aozora.gr.jp/cards/000093/files/527_28271.html “Folk Customs and Legends Concerning Rabbits”] (from ‘Jūnishi Kō’, Iwanami Bunko, 1994, as available on Aozora Bunko).. === On “Iratsuko” === “Iratsuko (郎子)” is an honorific appended to the name. Although the term “Rōjo (Iratsume/Iratsuhime)” appears frequently in the historical texts (43 instances in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}), the usage of “Iratsuko” for Ujinowakiiratsuko occurs for only four individuals in the Kojiki{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}The other three are: the grandson of Emperor Ōjin (Ōrōko, also known as the son of [【意富富杼王】]), the crown prince of Emperor Nintoku (Hatabino Ōrōko, also known as Ōhishimo or Ōsōkō), and the crown prince of Emperor Keitai (Ōrōko).. This distinctive usage—neither the common “Mikoto” nor “Ō (king)” used for imperial heirs—has drawn scholarly attention. Some argue that “Iratsuko” may have been used as a nickname, while others see it as a counterpart to “Rōjo”{{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}However, at present institutions such as {{ill|Uji Shrine|ja|宇治神社}} sometimes combine “Iratsuko” with “Mikoto,” rendering the name as “Ujinowakiiratsuko Mikoto.”. It is also noted that the element “Waki” preceding “Iratsuko” is considered a corruption of “Waka” (若){{Sfn|Kanazawa|2007}}. == Genealogy == === Kojiki and Nihon Shoki === (The naming follows the first appearance in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, with other texts such as the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} noted in parentheses.) According to the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}} and the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, Ujinowakiiratsuko was born a prince to Emperor Ōjin and the consort Miyanishitakuya-hime (宮主宅媛, also known as Miyanushiyakahaime or 宮主矢河枝比売) of the {{ill|Waerushi|ja|和珥氏}} (Maruni) clan{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, Emperor Ōjin Annals; {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}, 2nd year, March entry.. His maternal sisters include {{ill|Yatateno Hime-miko|ja|八田皇女}} (also known as Yata no Hime-miko or Yata Wakirōjo, later Empress) and Metori no Hime-miko (女鳥王). Ōsazaki ({{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇}}), born of Emperor Ōjin and {{ill|Nakatsuhime no Mikoto|ja|仲姫命}} (also known as Nakatsuhime or Nakachihime), was his half-brother. In addition, a related figure is the daughter of Miyanishitakuya-hime’s sister, Onabe-hime (小甂媛), who became known as Ujinowakiiratsuko Onna (菟道稚郎女皇女). There is no record in the historical texts regarding the wife or children of Ujinowakiiratsuko. {{Imperial Tomb Era}}
